title: Argonne and UIUC Demonstrate First On-Chip Coupling of Propagating Spin Waves to Superconducting Circuits
excerpt: Scientists from Argonne National Laboratory and UIUC have developed the first-of-its-kind hybrid circuit, integrating propagating spin waves with a superconducting resonator on a single chip. This innovation allows for strong coupling between microwave photons and spin waves, addressing issues of signal noise in quantum devices. By using a rare-earth-free YSGG substrate, the team achieved significant power isolation, paving the way for compact, on-chip microwave isolators for quantum circuits.
content:
In a research paper published in Physical Review Letters, scientists from Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) have demonstrated the first proof-of-concept hybrid circuit that couples propagating spin waves (magnons) in a magnetic thin film directly to a superconducting resonator on a single chip.

While superconducting circuits serve as standard microwave-processing components in quantum devices, they are susceptible to signal noise leaking backward through the circuit. Spin waves—magnetic excitations traveling through a material—naturally exhibit unidirectional (nonreciprocal) propagation under specific conditions. By fabricating a niobium nitride (NbN) superconducting coplanar waveguide resonator directly onto an epitaxial yttrium iron garnet (YIG) magnetic film, the team achieved strong coupling between microwave photons and propagating Damon-Eshbach and backward-volume spin wave modes.

To overcome cryogenic signal absorption—a long-standing bottleneck when integrating YIG films with low-temperature superconducting electronics—the researchers replaced standard gadolinium gallium garnet (GGG) substrates with rare-earth-free YSGG substrates. The resulting hybrid architecture achieves a power isolation of 4 dB at the degenerate mode transmission peak, laying the foundation for compact, on-chip microwave isolators that protect fragile quantum circuits without external bulk magnets.

The device fabrication was executed at the Center for Nanoscale Materials at Argonne. This hybrid platform builds upon prior research into spin-wave magnonic systems and advances the development of integrated, directional quantum optical and microwave interconnects.
